label: Control category (technical, managerial, operational, physical) vs control type (preventive, detective, ...)

mentor.diagnosis: You answered with the wrong axis. Every control has both a category and a type, and the question always asks for exactly one of them.
contrast: What kind of thing is it
What does it do about the event
Preventive, Deterrent, Detective, Corrective, Compensating, Directive
Type: could be deterrent, preventive or detective
mentor.rule: Category is what it is made of. Type is when it acts relative to the incident: before, during, or after.
mentor.tell: The words 'category' and 'type' in the stem are literal. Read which one is being asked before scanning the options.
mentor.trap: Both axes appear in the option list together, so a correct sounding word is always available on the wrong axis.

mentor.diagnosis: You picked preventive for a control that only discourages. A deterrent changes the attacker's mind, a preventive changes what is physically possible.
mentor.rule: Ask whether a determined attacker who ignores it is still stopped. If yes it is preventive, if no it is deterrent.
mentor.tell: Signs, lighting and visible cameras are the classic deterrent set.
mentor.trap: Deterrents do reduce incidents, so they feel preventive in effect. The exam classifies by mechanism, not by outcome.

mentor.diagnosis: You confused the control that stands in for another with the control that fixes damage afterwards.
contrast: The control you wanted is not possible
Legacy system cannot be patched, so it is isolated on its own VLAN
An exception in the risk register
What it substitutes for, not its own mechanism: session recording standing in for missing audit logs is compensating even though it detects
mentor.rule: Compensating substitutes for a missing control. Corrective repairs after the event.
mentor.tell: 'Cannot be patched', 'vendor no longer supports it', 'business will not accept the downtime' all set up a compensating control.
mentor.trap: Both are the answer to 'we have a problem', so both sound reactive. Compensating is chosen in advance and documented. And when the stem says a control was put in because the required one could not be, it is compensating, whatever its mechanism.

mentor.diagnosis: You picked a control that stops or fixes for one that only finds out. A detective control tells you something happened; it does not block it and it does not repair it.
contrast: Watches a copy of the traffic and raises an alert
Evidence afterwards; the visible camera is the deterrent
Blocks the action or the disclosure
mentor.rule: If the control's output is an alert, a log or a recording, it is detective. If its output is a blocked action, it is preventive. If its output is a repaired system, it is corrective.
mentor.tell: 'alerts', 'audits', 'reviews', 'monitors', 'records' set up detective; 'blocks', 'prevents', 'requires' set up preventive; 'restores', 'rebuilds' set up corrective.
mentor.trap: A detective control usually triggers a preventive or corrective response, so the pair gets collapsed. The exam classifies the control named in the stem, not the process around it.

label: Directive vs deterrent: a rule is not a barrier

mentor.diagnosis: You treated a rule that tells people what to do as a threat that discourages attackers, or as a barrier that stops them. A directive control instructs the compliant; a deterrent discourages the hostile; neither one physically prevents anything.
contrast: 'Visitors must sign in at reception' sign
Instructs who may proceed and how
Security awareness training, clean desk policy
A DLP rule that blocks the upload the policy forbids
The policy said no; the DLP makes no possible
mentor.rule: Directive is aimed at people who intend to comply and tells them how. Deterrent is aimed at people who intend not to and makes them reconsider. Preventive stops it regardless of intent.
mentor.tell: Policies, procedures, training and signs that give an instruction are directive. Signs, lighting and cameras that announce a consequence are deterrent.
mentor.trap: Both can be a sign on a door. Read what the sign says: an instruction is directive, a warning is deterrent. And a policy forbidding something has not prevented it; a control that enforces the policy has.

label: Managerial vs operational vs technical control category

mentor.diagnosis: You put a control in the category of the thing it protects or the team that owns it, rather than the kind of thing it is. Category is about the mechanism: a decision, a person doing something, or a system enforcing something.
contrast: A decision or a document that governs
Risk assessment, security policy, a written procedure, vendor review, change approval
Guard patrols, awareness training, an analyst reviewing logs, following the incident response procedure
A system enforcing without a person in the loop
mentor.rule: Ask who or what carries the control out. Management deciding is managerial, people doing is operational, a system doing is technical, matter in the way is physical.
mentor.tell: 'Policy', 'assessment', 'plan', 'documented procedure' point to managerial; 'training', 'patrol', 'review', 'performs', 'follows the procedure' point to operational.
mentor.trap: Training is about technical topics and is delivered by IT, so it reads as technical. It is people performing a process, which is operational. A procedure document is managerial; carrying it out is operational.
